So the code is a bijection between labelled trees and sequences of length n−2 over n labels, which proves Cayley's formula

#{labelled trees on n vertices}=nn−2.
A vertex's degree is one more than the number of times it appears in the code, so leaves are exactly the labels that never appear. `labelledTrees(n)` is a [family](https://ratmath.com/discrete/enumeration.html) numbered by code, so ranking, unranking and uniform random trees come for free; the tests check that it lists all 64=1296 trees on six vertices, each once, and that nn−2 agrees with the matrix-tree count for Kn​.

### Try it

```js
// Cayley two ways: the matrix-tree theorem on K_n, and n^(n-2).
for (let n = 2; n <= 8; n++) PRINT("n =", n, " Kirchhoff:", spanningTreeCount(complete(n)), " Cayley:", BigInt(n) ** BigInt(n - 2));

// A road network with exact costs: Kruskal and Prim agree.
const roads = graph("A-B:7/2 A-C:2 B-C:3/2 B-D:5 C-D:4 C-E:6 D-E:1 D-F:9/4 E-F:3");
const k = minimumSpanningTree(roads), p = minimumSpanningTree(roads, { method: "prim" });
PRINT("Kruskal:", String(k.weight), k.edges.map((e) => e.from + e.to).join(" "));
PRINT("Prim:   ", String(p.weight), p.edges.map((e) => e.from + e.to).join(" "));

// Prüfer codes: a random tree, its code, and the degrees read off from the code.
const t = randomTree(9, rng("prufer"));
const code = prufer(t);
PRINT("tree:", String(t));
PRINT("code:", code.join(" "));
PRINT("degree of each vertex = 1 + appearances in the code:", t.vertices().sort((a, b) => a - b).every((v) => t.degree(v) === 1 + code.filter((x) => x === v).length));

// How many labelled trees on 7 vertices are paths? stars? Count by walking the family.
let paths = 0, stars = 0;
for (const tr of labelledTrees(7)) { const ds = tr.degreeSequence(); if (ds[0] === 2) paths++; if (ds[0] === 6) stars++; }
[`paths: ${paths} (7!/2 = ${5040 / 2})`, `stars: ${stars}`]
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/discrete/matchings-flows.html

Graph theory

## Matchings and flows

A matching pairs vertices along edges; a flow sends material through a network. In both, the best answer comes with a short proof that nothing better exists: a Tutte–Berge set, a König cover, dual prices, or a cut.

### Maximum matching in any graph

```js
import { graph, star, maximumMatching } from "@ratmath/discrete";

const g = graph("a-b b-c c-a c-d d-e e-f f-d");   // two triangles joined by an edge
const m = maximumMatching(g);
m.edges;          // [["a","b"], ["c","d"], ["e","f"]]: perfect
maximumMatching(star(5)).certificate;
// { set: [0], oddComponents: [[1],[2],[3],[4],[5]], bound: 1 }
```

Edmonds' blossom algorithm grows alternating trees and shrinks odd cycles. The certificate is the Tutte–Berge formula: for any set U of vertices, with odd(G−U) the number of odd components left when U is removed,

ν(G)=U⊆Vmin​21​(∣V∣+∣U∣−odd(G−U)).
Each odd component must send a vertex to U to be matched completely, and U has only ∣U∣ vertices. The algorithm returns a U where the bound equals the matching size (from the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition), and `check()` recomputes both sides from the graph alone.

### Bipartite graphs: König and Hall

```js
import { bipartiteMatching } from "@ratmath/discrete";
bipartiteMatching(graph("a-x a-y b-x c-x"), { left: ["a", "b", "c"] });
// size 2, cover ["a", "x"], hall { set: ["c", "b"], neighbours: ["x"] }
```

In a bipartite graph the largest matching equals the smallest vertex cover (König), and a side can be matched completely exactly when every set S of its vertices has at least ∣S∣ neighbours (Hall). When it cannot, the answer names a set S with ∣N(S)∣.

### Assignment and stable matching

```js
import { assignment, stableMatching } from "@ratmath/discrete";
const a = assignment([[4, 1, 3], [2, 0, 5], [3, 2, 2]]);
a.assignment;   // [1, 0, 2]: row 0 takes column 1, …
a.cost;         // 5, with rowPrices [2, 1, 2] and columnPrices [1, −1, 0]
stableMatching({ a: ["x", "y", "z"], b: ["y", "x", "z"], c: ["x", "y", "z"] },
               { x: ["b", "a", "c"], y: ["a", "b", "c"], z: ["a", "b", "c"] }).matching;
// { a: "x", b: "y", c: "z" }, with no blocking pair
```

The assignment problem is a linear program whose optimum is always a permutation. Its dual prices ui​+vj​≤cij​, with equality on the chosen cells, prove the cost is least: any assignment costs at least ∑ui​+∑vj​. Gale–Shapley's proposal algorithm gives the stable matching best for the proposers.

### Maximum flow and minimum cut

```js
import { digraph, maxFlow } from "@ratmath/discrete";
const f = maxFlow(digraph("s>a:3 s>b:2 a>b:1 a>t:2 b>t:3"), "s", "t");
f.value;        // 5
f.cut.source;   // ["s"]: the cut {s→a, s→b} has capacity 5 too
maxFlow(graph("s-a:1/2 a-t:1/3 s-t:1"), "s", "t").value;   // 4/3, exactly
```

Edmonds–Karp augments along shortest paths in the residual network. When no augmenting path is left, the vertices still reachable from the source form a cut whose capacity equals the flow, which is the max-flow min-cut theorem: no flow exceeds any cut, so both are optimal. Capacities are exact fractions, so the answer is too.

### Try it

```js
// Matching size against brute force on random graphs, and the certificate.
const r = rng("matchings");
for (let t = 0; t < 5; t++) {
  const g = randomGraph(10, "1/4", r);
  const m = maximumMatching(g);
  PRINT(`${g.edges().length} edges: ν = ${m.size}, Tutte set [${m.certificate.set.join(", ")}], ${m.certificate.oddComponents.length} odd components, check:`, m.check().ok);
}
// Menger: the number of edge-disjoint paths between two vertices of the cube
const Q = hypercube(3);
PRINT("edge-disjoint paths in Q3:", String(maxFlow(Q, Q.vertices()[0], Q.vertices()[7]).value));
maximumMatching(petersen()).perfect
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/discrete/colouring.html

Graph theory

## Colouring and cliques

Colour the vertices so that neighbours differ. The fewest colours that work is the chromatic number χ(G); the number of ways to do it with k colours is a polynomial in k.

### The chromatic number

```js
import { petersen, wheel, chromaticNumber, greedyColouring, isProperColouring } from "@ratmath/discrete";

const c = chromaticNumber(petersen());
c.number;       // 3
c.lowerBound;   // { kind: "odd-cycle", cycle: [...], note: "an odd cycle cannot be coloured with two colours" }
chromaticNumber(wheel(5)).lowerBound;   // { kind: "search", note: "no 3-colouring exists: …" }
isProperColouring(petersen(), greedyColouring(petersen()));   // { ok: true, clash: null }
```

An upper bound is a colouring, which anyone can check. A lower bound needs an argument: a clique of size k needs k colours, an odd cycle needs three, and otherwise the record that an exhaustive DSATUR search with k−1 colours failed. The wheel with five spokes has no K4​, yet needs four colours: the rim is an odd cycle and the hub sees all of it.

### The chromatic polynomial

```js
import { chromaticPolynomial, cycleGraph } from "@ratmath/discrete";
chromaticPolynomial(cycleGraph(5)).toString();   // "k^5 − 5k^4 + 10k^3 − 10k^2 + 4k"
const P = chromaticPolynomial(petersen());
P.at(3);    // 120n
P.at(4);    // 12960n
```

For an edge e, colourings of G−e either give the ends different colours (colourings of G) or the same (colourings of G/e, with e contracted). So

P(G,k)=P(G−e,k)−P(G/e,k),
down to edgeless graphs with P=kn. For a cycle this gives P(Cn​,k)=(k−1)n+(−1)n(k−1). The recursion is memoised on graph shape, which keeps graphs like Petersen quick.

### Cliques and independent sets

```js
import { maximumClique, maximalCliques, maximumIndependentSet, graph } from "@ratmath/discrete";
maximumClique(petersen());                    // ["1,2", "3,4"]: Petersen has no triangle
maximumIndependentSet(petersen());            // 4 vertices
maximalCliques(graph("a-b b-c c-a c-d"));     // [["a","b","c"], ["d","c"]] (Bron–Kerbosch)
```

ω(G)≤χ(G), and χ(G)≥n/α(G) since each colour class is independent. The Petersen graph has α=4, so it needs at least ⌈10/4⌉=3 colours.

### Try it

```js
// The chromatic polynomial against counting colourings one by one.
const g = graph("a-b b-c c-d d-a a-c d-e");
const P = chromaticPolynomial(g);
PRINT("P(k) =", P.toString());
const vs = g.vertices();
for (const k of [1, 2, 3, 4]) {
  let n = 0;
  for (const col of words(k, vs.length)) {
    const c = new Map(vs.map((v, i) => [v, col[i]]));
    if (isProperColouring(g, c).ok) n++;
  }
  PRINT(`k = ${k}: polynomial ${P.at(k)}, counted ${n}`);
}
PRINT("χ =", chromaticNumber(g).number, " clique", maximumClique(g).join(""));
chromaticPolynomial(cycleGraph(6)).toString()
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/discrete/planarity.html

Graph theory

## Planarity

A graph is planar when it can be drawn in the plane without crossings. Kuratowski's theorem says the only obstructions are subdivisions of K5​ and K3,3​, so every answer here comes with evidence: faces for yes, one of those two subgraphs for no.

### Yes, with faces

```js
import { complete, planarity, isPlanar, hypercube, platonic } from "@ratmath/discrete";

planarity(complete(4));
// { planar: true, faces: [[[3,1,4], [4,3,2], [1,4,2], [2,3,1]]], edges: 6, vertices: 4 }
isPlanar(platonic("icosahedron"));   // true
isPlanar(hypercube(4));              // false
```

Each 2-connected block is embedded by the Demoucron–Malgrange–Pertuiset algorithm: start from a cycle, and repeatedly route a piece of the remaining graph through a face that holds all its attachment points, choosing a piece that fits in the fewest faces first. Faces are listed per block. Euler's formula is the check on every block:

V−E+F=2.
For K4​: 4−6+4=2.

### No, with a Kuratowski subgraph

```js
import { petersen, checkKuratowski } from "@ratmath/discrete";
const r = planarity(petersen());
r.kuratowski.kind;     // "K3,3"
r.kuratowski.branch;   // the six branch vertices
r.kuratowski.paths;    // nine paths joining them, internally disjoint
checkKuratowski(petersen(), r.kuratowski).ok;   // true
```

When the embedding fails, edges are deleted one at a time while the graph stays non-planar. What is left is edge-minimal non-planar, and by Kuratowski's theorem it is a subdivision of K5​ or K3,3​: the vertices of degree three or four are the branch vertices and the rest lie on paths between them. `checkKuratowski` confirms the paths use real edges, are disjoint apart from their ends, and join the right pairs.

### Quick counting arguments

A simple planar graph with V≥3 has E≤3V−6, since every face has at least three edges and each edge borders two faces. Without triangles it is E≤2V−4. So K5​ (10 > 9) and K3,3​ (9 > 8) are out at once; Petersen has 15 edges, within both bounds, and needs the search.

### Try it

```js
// Planar or not, with the evidence, for some well-known graphs.
for (const [name, g] of [["K5", complete(5)], ["K3,3", completeBipartite(3, 3)], ["Q3", hypercube(3)], ["Q4", hypercube(4)], ["dodecahedron", platonic("dodecahedron")], ["K2,7", completeBipartite(2, 7)], ["Petersen", petersen()]]) {
  const r = planarity(g);
  if (r.planar) {
    const F = r.faces.reduce((s, b) => s + b.length, 0);
    PRINT(name.padEnd(13), "planar:", r.faces.length, "block(s),", F, "faces; V − E + F per block =", r.faces.map((f) => g.vertices().length - g.edges().length + f.length).join(","));
  } else PRINT(name.padEnd(13), "not planar:", r.kuratowski.kind, "subdivision with", r.kuratowski.edges.length, "edges, check", checkKuratowski(g, r.kuratowski).ok);
}
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/discrete/isomorphism-spectra.html

Graph theory

## Isomorphism and spectra

When are two graphs the same up to renaming, and what symmetries does one graph have? Colour refinement and backtracking answer both for small graphs. The eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix, computed exactly, give invariants that count walks and spanning trees.

### Isomorphism

```js
import { isomorphism, petersen, kneser, cycleGraph, graph, pathGraph, star } from "@ratmath/discrete";

isomorphism(petersen(), kneser(5, 2)).isomorphic;   // true, with the map
isomorphism(cycleGraph(6), graph("a-b b-c c-a d-e e-f f-d")).reason;
// "colour refinement … splits the vertices differently": C6 against two triangles
isomorphism(pathGraph(4), star(3)).reason;   // "degree sequences differ: (2, 2, 1, 1) against (3, 1, 1, 1)"
```

Cheap invariants go first: vertex and edge counts, degree sequences. Then colour refinement (1-dimensional Weisfeiler–Leman): colour each vertex by its degree, then by its colour together with the multiset of its neighbours' colours, until nothing splits. An isomorphism must keep colours, so different class sizes prove there is none, and equal ones cut the backtracking search down. A "yes" is checked edge by edge.

### Automorphisms

```js
import { automorphisms, hypercube } from "@ratmath/discrete";
const a = automorphisms(petersen());
a.order;           // 120n: the symmetric group S5 acting on 2-subsets
a.orbits.length;   // 1: vertex-transitive
automorphisms(hypercube(3)).order;   // 48n
```

The group is built as a chain of stabilisers: fix a vertex, find one automorphism to each vertex of its orbit, then fix the next vertex. By the orbit–stabiliser theorem

∣Aut(G)∣=i∏​∣orbit of vi​ in Gv1​…vi−1​​∣,
so few generators give the order exactly. Up to order 50,000 the group also comes as a `PermGroup` from `@ratmath/algebraic`, whose own order is compared with the product. The Frucht graph is 3-regular yet has only the identity.

### Spectra

```js
import { spectrum, walks, spanningTreesFromSpectrum, spanningTreeCount } from "@ratmath/discrete";
spectrum(petersen()).toString();                     // "−2 (×4), 1 (×5), 3"
spectrum(hypercube(3)).toString();                   // "−3, −1 (×3), 1 (×3), 3"
spectrum(cycleGraph(5)).toString();                  // the values 2 cos(2πk/5), with √5
spanningTreesFromSpectrum(petersen());               // 2000n, as spanningTreeCount gives
walks(cycleGraph(5), 5).closed;                      // 10n closed walks of length 5
```

The characteristic polynomial det(xI−A) is computed over the integers by the Faddeev–LeVerrier recursion, and its roots are found exactly with `@ratmath/algebraic`. A symmetric matrix has only real eigenvalues, which is checked. The number of closed walks of length k is trAk=∑λik​. For the Laplacian L=D−A with eigenvalues 0=μ1​≤μ2​≤⋯≤μn​, the matrix-tree theorem gives the number of spanning trees:

τ(G)=n1​μ2​μ3​⋯μn​,
which is read off the coefficient of x in the Laplacian's characteristic polynomial, with no root-finding needed.

### Try it

```js
// Cospectral but not isomorphic: K1,4 and C4 + K1 share the spectrum {−2, 0, 0, 0, 2}.
const s1 = star(4), s2 = graph("a-b b-c c-d d-a e");
PRINT(spectrum(s1).toString(), " | ", spectrum(s2).toString());
PRINT("isomorphic?", isIsomorphic(s1, s2), "—", isomorphism(s1, s2).reason);
// Symmetry of the Platonic solids' skeletons
for (const n of ["tetrahedron", "cube", "octahedron", "dodecahedron", "icosahedron"]) {
  const g = platonic(n);
  PRINT(n.padEnd(13), "|Aut| =", String(automorphisms(g).order).padStart(4), " spectrum", spectrum(g).toString());
}
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/discrete/linear-programming.html

Optimisation and games

## Linear programming

Maximise or minimise a linear function subject to linear inequalities. The simplex method here works in exact fractions, and every answer arrives with the evidence that proves it: an optimum with its dual prices, an impossibility with a Farkas combination, an unbounded problem with a ray.

### A first problem

```js
// A workshop makes chairs (£30 profit) and tables (£50) from wood and labour.
import { linearProgram } from "@ratmath/discrete";

const plan = linearProgram({
  maximize: { chairs: 30, tables: 50 },
  constraints: [
    [{ chairs: 2, tables: 4 }, "<=", 100, "wood"],
    [{ chairs: 3, tables: 2 }, "<=", 90, "labour"],
  ],
});

String(plan);     // "optimal: 1350 at chairs = 20, tables = 15"
plan.prices;      // { wood: 45/4, labour: 5/2 }: what one more unit of each is worth
plan.binding;     // ["wood", "labour"]: both are used up
plan.check();     // true: the prices prove that 1350 is the best possible
```

A linear program asks for x maximising c⋅x subject to constraints ai​⋅x≤bi​ (or ≥, or =) and, unless a variable is declared `free`, x≥0. The feasible set is a convex polyhedron, and if the optimum exists it is reached at a vertex. The simplex method walks from vertex to vertex along edges, improving the objective at each step. Here each step is an exact pivot on a tableau of fractions, and Bland's rule (always the lowest-numbered improving column) guarantees the walk never cycles.

### Why the prices are a proof

Multiply each constraint by a non-negative price yi​ and add. If the combined left side is at least the objective, coefficient by coefficient, then for every feasible x

c⋅x≤i∑​yi​(ai​⋅x)≤i∑​yi​bi​=b⋅y.
That is weak duality: any such y gives an upper bound. For the workshop, y=(45/4,5/2) gives 2⋅445​+3⋅25​=30 and 4⋅445​+2⋅25​=50, exactly the profits, and a bound of 100⋅445​+90⋅25​=1350. The plan reaches 1350, so nothing does better. Strong duality says such a matching pair always exists when there is an optimum, and the simplex method finds both at once.

`check()` uses none of the simplex code. It confirms that x satisfies every constraint, that the prices have the right signs, that they cover the objective, and that c⋅x=b⋅y. The prices are also sensitivities: one more unit of wood raises the profit by exactly 45/4, as long as the same constraints stay binding.

### Minimising, with fractions

```js
const diet = linearProgram({
  minimize: { bread: "1/2", milk: "3/4", beans: "6/5" },     // cost per portion
  constraints: [
    [{ bread: 4, milk: 8, beans: 7 }, ">=", 30, "protein"],
    [{ bread: 10, milk: 3, beans: 20 }, ">=", 60, "iron"],
    [{ bread: 300, milk: 150, beans: 200 }, ">=", 2000, "energy"],
    [{ milk: 1 }, "<=", 4, "milk limit"],
  ],
});
String(diet);   // "optimal: 65/18 at bread = 115/18, milk = 5/9, beans = 0"
diet.prices;    // { protein: 1/12, iron: 0, energy: 1/1800, "milk limit": 0 }
String(diet.problem);   // the problem written out, as the solver read it
```

Coefficients can be fractions (`"6/5"`), decimals (`"0.25"` or `0.25`) or whole numbers. Variables can be named through objects, as here, or listed by position: `maximize: [3, 2]` with rows such as `[[1, 1], "<=", 4]`.

### When there is no answer

```js
const none = linearProgram({ maximize: { x: 1, y: 1 }, constraints: [
  [{ x: 1, y: 2 }, "<=", 4, "a"], [{ x: 3, y: 1 }, "<=", 6, "b"], [{ x: 1, y: 1 }, ">=", 3, "c"] ] });
none.status;    // "infeasible"
none.farkas;    // [2/5, 1/5, −1]: (2/5)·a + (1/5)·b says x + y ≤ 14/5, but c says x + y ≥ 3

const open = linearProgram({ maximize: { x: 1, y: 1 }, constraints: [
  [{ x: 1, y: -1 }, "<=", 2], [{ x: -1, y: 1 }, "<=", 4] ] });
open.status;    // "unbounded"
open.x;         // [2, 0]: a feasible point
open.ray;       // [1, 1]: from it, move in this direction for ever
```

An infeasible problem comes with a Farkas certificate: multipliers (non-negative on ≤ rows, non-positive on ≥ rows) whose combination of the constraints has left side ≥0 on every x≥0 but a negative right side. No point can satisfy that, so none can satisfy the constraints. Farkas' lemma says such multipliers exist whenever a system has no solution; phase one of the simplex method finds them. An unbounded problem comes with a feasible point and a ray d with ai​⋅d of the right sign for every constraint and c⋅d>0. Both are checked by `check()` in the same way as an optimum.

### The transportation problem

```js
const t = transportation([20, 30], [10, 25, 15], [[8, 6, 10], [9, 12, 13]]);
t.cost;   // 465
t.plan;   // [[0, 20, 0], [10, 5, 15]]: warehouse 1 sends 20 to store 2, …
t.lp.check();   // true: the prices prove no plan is cheaper
```

Sources with supplies si​ ship to sinks with demands dj​ at cost cij​ per unit. With xij​ the amount from i to j, minimise ∑cij​xij​ subject to ∑j​xij​=si​ and ∑i​xij​=dj​. `transportation(supply, demand, cost)` builds that program, solves it exactly and returns the shipping table. If total supply exceeds total demand, a dummy sink with cost 0 takes the rest (`leftover` says how much stays at each source); if demand exceeds supply, a dummy source records the `unmet` demand. The duals of the source and sink rows are the potentials ui​, vj​ of the stepping-stone method: every route has cij​−ui​−vj​≥0, which is the optimality certificate.

### Try it

```js
// A workshop makes chairs (£30 profit) and tables (£50) from wood and labour.
const plan = linearProgram({
  maximize: { chairs: 30, tables: 50 },
  constraints: [
    [{ chairs: 2, tables: 4 }, "<=", 100, "wood"],
    [{ chairs: 3, tables: 2 }, "<=", 90, "labour"],
  ],
});
PRINT(String(plan));
PRINT("prices:", Object.entries(plan.prices).map(([k, v]) => `${k} ${v}`).join(", "));
// the proof by hand: the priced constraints cover the profits and bound the total
const [w, l] = plan.dual;
PRINT("chairs:", String(w.multiply(new Rational(2n)).add(l.multiply(new Rational(3n)))), " tables:", String(w.multiply(new Rational(4n)).add(l.multiply(new Rational(2n)))));
PRINT("bound b·y =", String(w.multiply(new Rational(100n)).add(l.multiply(new Rational(90n)))));
// one more unit of wood is worth exactly the price of wood
const more = linearProgram({ maximize: { chairs: 30, tables: 50 },
  constraints: [[{ chairs: 2, tables: 4 }, "<=", 101, "wood"], [{ chairs: 3, tables: 2 }, "<=", 90, "labour"]] });
PRINT("with 101 wood:", String(more.value), " gain", String(more.value.subtract(plan.value)));
// A transportation problem with more supply than demand: a dummy sink absorbs the rest.
const t = transportation([20, 40], [10, 25, 15], [[8, 6, 10], [9, 12, 13]]);
PRINT("cost", String(t.cost), " plan", JSON.stringify(t.plan.map((r) => r.map(String))), " left at each source", t.leftover.map(String).join(", "));
plan.check()
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/discrete/integer-programs.html

Optimisation and games

## Integer programs

When the answer must be whole numbers (items packed, machines bought, people assigned), rounding the linear optimum is not enough. Branch and bound splits the problem until every piece is either whole, impossible, or provably no better than what has been found.

### A knapsack

```js
import { integerProgram } from "@ratmath/discrete";

const pack = integerProgram({
  maximize: { a: 8, b: 11, c: 6, d: 4 },                    // values
  constraints: [
    [{ a: 5, b: 7, c: 4, d: 3 }, "<=", 14],                   // weights, capacity 14
    [{ a: 1 }, "<=", 1], [{ b: 1 }, "<=", 1], [{ c: 1 }, "<=", 1], [{ d: 1 }, "<=", 1],
  ],
});
String(pack);   // "optimal: 21 at a = 0, b = 1, c = 1, d = 1 (13 subproblems; relaxation 22)"

// the same 0–1 knapsack in one call: binary adds x ≤ 1 and wholeness for each variable
integerProgram({ maximize: { a: 8, b: 11, c: 6, d: 4 }, constraints: [[{ a: 5, b: 7, c: 4, d: 3 }, "<=", 14]] }, { binary: true });
```

The linear relaxation drops the requirement that the variables be whole and is solved exactly. Its optimum bounds the integer optimum: here no packing is worth more than 22. If its solution is already whole, it is the answer. Otherwise some variable has a fractional value v, and every integer solution has either x≤⌊v⌋ or x≥⌊v⌋+1. Each case is a new linear program. A branch is closed when its relaxation is infeasible, whole, or no better than the best whole solution found so far.

### Rounding is not enough

```js
const r = integerProgram({ maximize: [5, 4], constraints: [[[6, 4], "<=", 24], [[1, 2], "<=", 6]] });
r.relaxation.solution;   // { x1: 3, x2: 3/2 }: the linear optimum, worth 21
String(r);               // "optimal: 20 at x1 = 4, x2 = 0 (5 subproblems; relaxation 21)"
```

Rounding the relaxation's (3,3/2) gives (3,1), worth 19, or the infeasible (3,2). The best integer point, (4,0), is not near it. Integer programming is NP-hard in general, so the search can grow exponentially. This solver is for small problems and for teaching; it refuses with `"too-hard"` beyond `maxNodes` subproblems (20,000 by default). Pass `integer: ["x"]` to require only some variables to be whole, and `binary: true` (or a list of names) to make variables 0 or 1.

The `check()` of an integer result confirms feasibility and wholeness. Unlike a linear optimum it carries no short proof of optimality: that rests on the search, and the test suite compares the search with every integer point of hundreds of small random problems.

### Try it

```js
// Branch and bound against brute force on a small problem.
const P = { maximize: [3, 5], constraints: [[[2, 3], "<=", 12], [[-1, 1], "<=", "3/2"], [[1, 0], "<=", 5]] };
const ip = integerProgram(P);
PRINT(String(ip));
PRINT("relaxation:", String(ip.relaxation));
let best = null, at = null;
for (let x = 0; x <= 6; x++) for (let y = 0; y <= 6; y++) {
  if (!isFeasible(P, [x, y])) continue;
  const v = 3 * x + 5 * y;
  if (best === null || v > best) { best = v; at = [x, y]; }
}
PRINT("brute force:", best, "at", at.join(", "));
// A 0–1 knapsack with binary: true, against all 2^5 choices.
const values = [10, 13, 7, 8, 4], weights = [5, 6, 4, 5, 2];
const k = integerProgram({ maximize: values, constraints: [[weights, "<=", 13]] }, { binary: true });
let bestK = 0;
for (let m = 0; m < 32; m++) {
  let w = 0, v = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++) if ((m >> i) & 1) { w += weights[i]; v += values[i]; }
  if (w <= 13 && v > bestK) bestK = v;
}
PRINT("knapsack:", String(k), " brute force:", bestK);
ip.check()
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/discrete/matrix-games.html

Optimisation and games

## Matrix games

In a zero-sum game one player's gain is the other's loss. Von Neumann's theorem says each player has a mixed strategy that guarantees the same number, the value of the game. Linear programming finds both strategies and the value, here as exact fractions.

### Rock, paper, scissors

```js
import { matrixGame, saddlePoints } from "@ratmath/discrete";

const names = ["rock", "paper", "scissors"];
const rps = matrixGame([[0, -1, 1], [1, 0, -1], [-1, 1, 0]], { rows: names, columns: names });
String(rps);   // "value 0; row plays rock 1/3, paper 1/3, scissors 1/3; column plays rock 1/3, …"
rps.fair;      // true
rps.check();   // true
```

The matrix A lists what the column player pays the row player: Aij​ when row i meets column j. If the row player mixes with probabilities p and the column player with q, the expected payment is p⊤Aq. The row player wants it large and the column player small.

### The minimax theorem

A mixture p guarantees minj​(p⊤A)j​, the worst it earns against any column. A mixture q caps the row player at maxi​(Aq)i​. Every guarantee is at most every cap, and von Neumann's theorem says the best guarantee equals the best cap:

pmax​qmin​p⊤Aq=qmin​pmax​p⊤Aq=v.
The row player's problem is a linear program: maximise v subject to (p⊤A)j​≥v for every column, ∑pi​=1, p≥0. Its dual is exactly the column player's problem, so one exact solve gives both strategies, and LP duality is the theorem. `check()` confirms the guarantee of p and the cap of q are both v: neither player can do better, so no further proof is needed.

```js
const g = matrixGame([[3, -1], [-2, 1]]);
String(g);                          // "value 1/7; row plays r1 3/7, r2 4/7; column plays c1 2/7, c2 5/7"
g.guarantee(["1/2", "1/2"]);        // 0: a fifty-fifty row player can be held to 0
g.cap(["1/2", "1/2"]);              // 1
g.guarantee();                      // 1/7, and g.cap() is 1/7 too
```

For a 2×2 game without a saddle point the optimal p makes the column player indifferent: 3p−2(1−p)=−p+(1−p) gives p=3/7.

### Saddle points

```js
saddlePoints([[4, 2, 3], [1, 0, 5], [3, 1, 2]]);   // [{ row: 0, column: 1, value: 2 }]
matrixGame([[4, 2, 3], [1, 0, 5], [3, 1, 2]]).value;   // 2: pure strategies suffice
```

An entry that is the smallest in its row and the largest in its column is a saddle point. There, pure strategies are optimal and the value is that entry. Many games have none, like rock, paper, scissors, and then mixing is essential.

### Morra

In two-finger Morra each player shows one or two fingers and calls a guess of the total. A player who guesses right and whose opponent guesses wrong wins the total. Keeping the four sensible strategies (show 1 and call 2 or 3; show 2 and call 3 or 4) gives a fair game with a curious answer:

```js
const s = ["1,2", "1,3", "2,3", "2,4"];   // fingers shown, total called
const morra = matrixGame([[0, 2, -3, 0], [-2, 0, 0, 3], [3, 0, 0, -4], [0, -3, 4, 0]], { rows: s, columns: s });
String(morra);   // "value 0; row plays 1,3 4/7, 2,3 3/7; column plays 1,3 3/5, 2,3 2/5"
```

Optimal strategies need not be unique. Here any mixture of "1,3" and "2,3" between 4/7:3/7 and 3/5:2/5 is optimal; the simplex method returns one vertex of that set.

### Try it

```js
// Random games: the guarantee and the cap always meet.
const r = rng("matrix games");
for (let t = 0; t < 5; t++) {
  const A = Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => Array.from({ length: 4 }, () => r.between(-5, 5)));
  const g = matrixGame(A);
  PRINT(A.map((row) => row.join(" ")).join(" | "), "→ value", String(g.value), " guarantee", String(g.guarantee()), " cap", String(g.cap()));
}
// shifting every payoff by 10 shifts the value by 10 and leaves the strategies alone
const g = matrixGame([[3, -1], [-2, 1]]);
const h = matrixGame([[13, 9], [8, 11]]);
PRINT(String(g.value), "→", String(h.value), " same row strategy:", g.row.every((v, i) => v.equals(h.row[i])));
g.check()
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/discrete/bimatrix-games.html

Optimisation and games

## Bimatrix games

When the players' interests are not exactly opposed, each has their own payoff matrix, and the solution is a Nash equilibrium: a pair of strategies where neither player gains by changing alone. A game can have several. Here they are found exactly and each one is checked.

### The prisoner's dilemma

```js
import { bimatrixGame } from "@ratmath/discrete";

const c = ["cooperate", "defect"];
const pd = bimatrixGame([[3, 0], [5, 1]], [[3, 5], [0, 1]], { rows: c, columns: c });
pd.dominance();
// { rows: ["defect"], columns: ["defect"], steps: [
//     { player: "row", removed: "cooperate", by: { defect: 1 } }, { player: "column", … } ] }
pd.equilibria().map(String);   // ["(defect; defect) paying 1 and 1"]
```

A holds the row player's payoffs and B the column player's. A strategy is strictly dominated if another does better against everything the opponent might do; no rational player uses it, so it can be removed, and the removal may expose more. In the prisoner's dilemma defecting dominates for both, so both defect and get 1 each, though cooperating would give each 3.

### Dominated by a mixture

```js
const g = bimatrixGame([[3, 0], [0, 3], [1, 1]], [[1, 0], [0, 1], [0, 0]],
                       { rows: ["top", "middle", "bottom"], columns: ["left", "right"] });
g.dominance({ pureOnly: true }).rows;   // ["top", "middle", "bottom"]: no pure strategy beats bottom
g.dominance().steps[0];                 // { player: "row", removed: "bottom", by: { top: 1/2, middle: 1/2 } }
```

Bottom pays 1 against either column. Neither top nor middle beats it everywhere, but the fifty-fifty mixture pays 3/2 against both. Whether some mixture strictly dominates a strategy is a small linear program (maximise the margin ε by which the mixture wins), solved exactly.

### Every equilibrium

```js
const chicken = bimatrixGame([[0, -1], [1, -10]], [[0, 1], [-1, -10]],
                             { rows: ["swerve", "straight"], columns: ["swerve", "straight"] });
const eq = chicken.equilibria();
eq.map(String);
// ["(swerve; straight) paying -1 and 1",
//  "(straight; swerve) paying 1 and -1",
//  "(9/10 swerve + 1/10 straight; 9/10 swerve + 1/10 straight) paying -1/10 and -1/10"]
eq.complete;    // true: the game is nondegenerate, so this is all of them
```

At an equilibrium each player mixes only over strategies that are best responses, so every strategy in the support pays the same. Support enumeration tries each pair of supports I,J of equal size, solves the indifference equations

j∈J∑​Aij​qj​=u (i∈I),i∈I∑​pi​Bij​=w (j∈J),∑pi​=∑qj​=1
exactly, and keeps the solutions that are positive on the supports and best responses overall. In a nondegenerate game (no mixture over k strategies has more than k best responses) equilibria have supports of equal size and this finds them all, and their number is odd. When an indifference system has a whole line of solutions the game is degenerate, it may have infinitely many equilibria, and the list is marked `complete: false`. The work grows like (mm+n​); beyond a million pairs of supports it refuses.

### Lemke–Howson

```js
chicken.lemkeHowson(0).toString();   // "(swerve; straight) paying -1 and 1"
chicken.lemkeHowson(1).toString();   // "(straight; swerve) paying 1 and -1"
```

The Lemke–Howson method finds one equilibrium by a path. Label each pure strategy; an equilibrium is a pair of points in two polytopes that together carry every label. Dropping one label k at the artificial starting point and pivoting, alternately in each polytope, to pick up the label just lost, follows a path that must end at an equilibrium. Different starting labels can reach different equilibria. The argument also proves that every game has an equilibrium, and that a nondegenerate game has an odd number of them; the test suite checks both on 200 random games.

### Try it

```js
// Random 3×3 games: count equilibria, check each, and see Lemke–Howson land on one.
const r = rng("bimatrix");
const M = () => Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => r.between(-9, 9)));
for (let t = 0; t < 6; t++) {
  const g = bimatrixGame(M(), M());
  const eq = g.equilibria();
  const lh = g.lemkeHowson(0);
  PRINT(`${eq.length} equilibri${eq.length === 1 ? "um" : "a"}${eq.complete ? "" : " (degenerate game)"};`, "all check:", eq.every((e) => e.check()),
        "; Lemke–Howson found:", String(lh));
}
bimatrixGame([[2, 0], [0, 1]], [[1, 0], [0, 2]]).equilibria().length
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/discrete/combinatorial-games.html

Optimisation and games

## Combinatorial games

Two players move in turn, everything is known, and whoever cannot move loses. Every impartial position is worth a nim heap, and every partizan position has a canonical value in Conway's sense: numbers, nimbers, up, and more.

### Nim and the Sprague–Grundy theorem

```js
import { nim, impartialGame, subtractionGame, mex } from "@ratmath/discrete";

nim([3, 4, 5]);   // nimSum 2n, losing false, winningMoves [{ heap: 0, from: 3n, to: 1n }]
const g = impartialGame((n) => [1, 2].filter((m) => m <= n).map((m) => n - m));
[0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].map(g.grundy).join("");   // "0120120"
subtractionGame([1, 3, 4], 30).period;           // { start: 0, length: 7 }
```

The Grundy value of a position is the smallest non-negative integer not among its options' values,

G(P)=mex{G(Q):P→Q},
and a position is lost for the player to move exactly when G(P)=0. The Sprague–Grundy theorem says a sum of games has value the nim-sum (bitwise XOR) of the parts, which is why nim is solved by XOR. Subtraction games with a finite set are eventually periodic; the period is found by looking for a repeat as long as the largest move.

### Partizan games

```js
import { cgame, starGame, up, down } from "@ratmath/discrete";
String(cgame([0], []));         // "1"
String(cgame([0], [1]));        // "1/2"
String(cgame([0], [0]));        // "*"
String(starGame(2).add(starGame(3)));   // "*": nimbers add by XOR
String(up().add(up()));         // "⇑"
up().compare(0);                // ">": up is positive …
up().compare(starGame(1));      // "‖": … yet confused with *
cgame([2], [-1]).outcome;       // "first player"
```

A game is G={GL∣GR}, its options for Left and for Right. G≥0 means Left wins moving second, and the order, sum and negation follow Conway's recursive definitions. Each game is reduced to canonical form by removing dominated options and bypassing reversible ones, so equal games print the same: {0∣1}=1/2, {0∣0}=∗, {0∣∗}=↑.

### Hackenbush

`partizanGame` computes the value of any position from the two players' move functions. In blue-red Hackenbush on a single stalk, the value is a binary fraction you can read off the colours:

```js
import { partizanGame } from "@ratmath/discrete";
const stalk = (s) => partizanGame(s,
  (p) => [...p].map((c, i) => (c === "B" ? p.slice(0, i) : null)).filter((x) => x !== null),
  (p) => [...p].map((c, i) => (c === "R" ? p.slice(0, i) : null)).filter((x) => x !== null));
String(stalk("BR"));     // "1/2"
String(stalk("BBRB"));   // "7/4"
```

### Backward induction

```js
import { backwardInduction } from "@ratmath/discrete";
const entry = { player: "A", moves: {
  in:  { player: "B", moves: { fight: { payoff: { A: -1, B: -1 } }, share: { payoff: { A: 1, B: 1 } } } },
  out: { payoff: { A: 0, B: 2 } } } };
backwardInduction(entry).path;   // ["in", "share"]: the threat to fight is not credible
```

In a finite game tree with perfect information, solving from the leaves up gives a subgame-perfect equilibrium. Ties are reported rather than broken silently.

### Try it

```js
// Sprague–Grundy at work: a sum of three different games.
const take12 = impartialGame((n) => [1, 2].filter((m) => m <= n).map((m) => n - m));
const sub = subtractionGame([1, 3, 4], 40).values;
const position = { take12: 7, subtract: 9, heap: 5 };
const values = [take12.grundy(7), sub[9], 5];
PRINT("Grundy values", values.join(", "), " nim-sum", values.reduce((a, b) => a ^ b));
// Numbers, nimbers and infinitesimals side by side
for (const G of [cgame([0], [1]), cgame(["1/2"], ["3/4"]), starGame(1).add(starGame(1)), up().add(starGame(1)), up().add(up()).add(down())]) {
  PRINT(String(G).padEnd(6), "compared with 0:", G.compare(0), " outcome:", G.outcome);
}
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/discrete/cooperative-voting.html

Optimisation and games

## Cooperative games and voting

When players can make binding agreements, the question is how to share what a coalition earns. When voters rank candidates, the question is how to choose. Both have several reasonable answers that can disagree, and here every answer is an exact fraction.

### The Shapley value

```js
import { cooperativeGame, shapley, core, inCore } from "@ratmath/discrete";

const glove = cooperativeGame(["L1", "L2", "R"],
  (S) => (S.includes("R") && (S.includes("L1") || S.includes("L2")) ? 1 : 0));
shapley(glove);   // { L1: 1/6, L2: 1/6, R: 2/3 }
```

A coalitional game assigns a worth v(S) to each coalition S. Player i's Shapley value is their average marginal contribution over all orders in which the players could arrive:

ϕi​=S∋i∑​n!∣S∣!(n−∣S∣−1)!​(v(S∪{i})−v(S)).
It is the only sharing rule that is efficient, symmetric, additive and gives nothing to a dummy.

### The core

```js
core(glove);   // { empty: false, allocation: { L1: 0, L2: 0, R: 1 } }
const majority = cooperativeGame(["a", "b", "c"], (S) => (S.length >= 2 ? 1 : 0));
core(majority);
// { empty: true, balanced: [{ab, 1/2}, {ac, 1/2}, {bc, 1/2}],
//   reason: "these coalitions, with these weights, cover every player exactly once and are worth 3/2 together, more than v(N) = 1" }
```

The core is the set of allocations no coalition can improve on by leaving: ∑i∈S​xi​≥v(S) for all S, with ∑xi​=v(N). It is found by exact linear programming. When it is empty, the dual gives a balanced collection (Bondareva–Shapley): coalitions with weights covering each player exactly once whose weighted worth exceeds v(N), a short proof that no allocation can satisfy them all.

`core` gives one allocation; `coreVertices(game)` gives them all. Every vertex of the core polytope makes x(N)=v(N) and n−1 independent coalition constraints tight, so each such system is solved exactly and kept when it satisfies every constraint. `kind` is `"empty"`, `"point"` or `"polytope"`, with the `dimension`. In the glove game with one left glove and two right ones, the right gloves compete and the core is the single point (1,0,0).

```js
const gloves = cooperativeGame(["L", "R1", "R2"], (S) => (S.includes("L") && S.length >= 2 ? 1 : 0));
coreVertices(gloves);   // { kind: "point", vertices: [{ L: 1, R1: 0, R2: 0 }], dimension: 0 }
```

### Voting power

```js
import { weightedVoting } from "@ratmath/discrete";
weightedVoting({ quota: 51, weights: { A: 49, B: 48, C: 3 } }).shapleyShubik;   // 1/3 each
```

With 49%, 48% and 3% of the votes and a simple majority, any two parties win, so all three have equal power. Banzhaf counts swings instead of orders; both are given.

### Choosing a winner

```js
import { plurality, borda, instantRunoff, condorcet } from "@ratmath/discrete";
const ballots = [{ ranking: ["A", "B", "C"], count: 8 }, { ranking: ["B", "C", "A"], count: 5 }, { ranking: ["C", "B", "A"], count: 4 }];
plurality(ballots).winners;      // ["A"]
borda(ballots).winners;          // ["B"]
instantRunoff(ballots).winners;  // ["B"]
condorcet(ballots).winner;       // "B": beats each other candidate head to head
condorcet([["a", "b", "c"], ["b", "c", "a"], ["c", "a", "b"]]).cycle;   // ["a", "b", "c", "a"]
```

Arrow's theorem says no ranked method with three or more candidates has every fairness property one would like, and small profiles like this one show methods disagreeing. A Condorcet cycle is reported as the cycle.

### Apportionment and fair division

```js
import { apportion, adjustedWinner } from "@ratmath/discrete";
apportion({ A: 6, B: 6, C: 2 }, 10).seats;   // { A: 4, B: 4, C: 2 }
apportion({ A: 6, B: 6, C: 2 }, 11).seats;   // { A: 5, B: 5, C: 1 }: the Alabama paradox
adjustedWinner({ house: 50, car: 20, boat: 30 }, { house: 40, car: 40, boat: 20 }).points;   // 520/9 each
```

Hamilton's method rounds quotas down and hands out the remaining seats by largest remainder; adding a seat can cost a state one. The divisor methods (Jefferson, Webster, Adams, Huntington–Hill) avoid that paradox but can violate quota. Adjusted winner splits at most one item and leaves both parties with equal points and no envy.

### Try it

```js
// The core of three games: one point, a segment, and empty.
const gloves = cooperativeGame(["L", "R1", "R2"], (S) => (S.includes("L") && S.length >= 2 ? 1 : 0));
const pair = cooperativeGame(["A", "B", "C"], (S) => (S.length === 3 ? 1 : S.join("") === "AB" ? 1 : 0));
const majority = cooperativeGame(["A", "B", "C"], (S) => (S.length >= 2 ? 1 : 0));
for (const [name, g] of [["gloves", gloves], ["A and B", pair], ["majority", majority]]) {
  const c = coreVertices(g);
  PRINT(name.padEnd(9), c.kind, "dimension", c.dimension, c.vertices.map((x) => JSON.stringify(Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(x).map(([k, v]) => [k, String(v)])))).join(" "));
}
// One profile, every method.
const r = rng("election");
const cands = ["A", "B", "C", "D"];
const ballots = Array.from({ length: 6 }, () => ({ ranking: r.shuffle(cands), count: r.between(1, 9) }));
for (const b of ballots) PRINT(String(b.count).padStart(2), "×", b.ranking.join(" > "));
PRINT("plurality      ", plurality(ballots).winners.join(", "));
PRINT("Borda          ", borda(ballots).winners.join(", "));
PRINT("instant runoff ", instantRunoff(ballots).winners.join(", "));
const c = condorcet(ballots);
PRINT("Condorcet      ", c.winner ?? `none, cycle ${c.cycle?.join(" → ")}`);
// The five apportionment methods on one census
const census = { North: 4729, South: 2611, East: 1802, West: 858 };
for (const m of ["hamilton", "jefferson", "webster", "adams", "huntington-hill"]) PRINT(m.padEnd(16), JSON.stringify(apportion(census, 20, { method: m }).seats, (k, v) => (typeof v === "bigint" ? Number(v) : v)));
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/discrete/relations-orders.html

Orders and structures

## Relations and orders

A relation is a set of ordered pairs. Whether it is reflexive, symmetric or transitive is a finite check, and when a property fails the answer names the pairs that break it. Partial orders get their own tools: Hasse diagrams, chains and antichains, linear extensions, and the Möbius function.

### Relations

```js
import { relation, fromPartition } from "@ratmath/discrete";

const R = relation([1, 2, 3, 4], [[1, 2], [2, 3]]);
R.properties().transitive;        // { holds: false, witness: [1, 2, 3] }: 1R2, 2R3, but not 1R3
String(R.transitiveClosure());    // "{(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)}"
relation([1, 2, 3], (a, b) => (a - b) % 2 === 0).classes();   // [[1, 3], [2]]
```

Each property comes with a witness when it fails: an element not related to itself, a pair whose reverse is missing, or the three elements that break transitivity. The transitive closure is computed by Warshall's algorithm. An equivalence relation and a partition are the same thing, and `classes()` and `fromPartition` go between them.

### Partial orders

```js
import { poset, divisorLattice } from "@ratmath/discrete";
const D = divisorLattice(60);
D.hasse().length;                   // 20 covering pairs
D.levels().map((l) => l.length);    // [1, 3, 4, 3, 1]
D.width();   // { width: 4, antichain: [4, 6, 10, 15], chains: [[1,2,4,12,60], [3,6,30], [5,10,20], [15]] }
```

A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive; `poset` takes generating pairs, closes them, and refuses a cycle with the two elements that would be equal. Dilworth's theorem says the largest antichain has the same size as the fewest chains covering the order. Both are found together from a maximum bipartite matching between "lower" and "upper" copies of the elements, so each is a certificate for the other.

### Linear extensions and the Möbius function

```js
import { booleanLattice, partitionLattice } from "@ratmath/discrete";
booleanLattice(3).countLinearExtensions();   // 48n
D.mobius(1, 30);                             // −1: the number-theoretic μ(30)
partitionLattice(4).mobius("1|2|3|4", "1234");   // −6 = (−1)^3·3!
```

A linear extension is a total order compatible with the partial one; they are counted by dynamic programming over down-sets. The Möbius function is defined by μ(x,x)=1 and ∑x≤z≤y​μ(x,z)=0 for x. It inverts sums over the order:

g(y)=x≤y∑​f(x)⟺f(y)=x≤y∑​μ(x,y)g(x),
which on divisors is Möbius inversion of number theory and on subsets is inclusion–exclusion.

### Lattices

```js
const N5 = poset(["0", "a", "b", "c", "1"], [["0", "a"], ["a", "b"], ["0", "c"], ["b", "1"], ["c", "1"]]);
N5.isLattice();         // { lattice: true }
N5.isDistributive();    // { distributive: false, witness: ["b", "a", "c"] }
```

A lattice has a meet and a join for every pair. It is distributive exactly when it contains neither the pentagon N5​ nor the diamond M3​; when the law x∧(y∨z)=(x∧y)∨(x∧z) fails, the three elements are given.

### Try it

```js
// Divisor lattices: width, chains, and Möbius against the number-theoretic μ.
const mu = (n) => { let m = 1; for (let p = 2; p * p <= n; p++) if (n % p === 0) { n /= p; if (n % p === 0) return 0; m = -m; } return n > 1 ? -m : m; };
for (const n of [12, 30, 36, 60, 210]) {
  const D = divisorLattice(n);
  const w = D.width();
  PRINT(`D(${n}): ${D.elements.length} divisors, width ${w.width} (antichain ${w.antichain.join(",")}), extensions ${D.countLinearExtensions()}, μ(1,${n}) = ${D.mobius(1, n)} vs ${mu(n)}`);
}
// Closures of a random relation
const r = rng("relation");
const R = relation([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], (a, b) => r.bool("1/4"));
PRINT(String(R));
PRINT(Object.entries(R.properties()).map(([k, v]) => `${k}: ${v.holds}`).join(", "));
PRINT("transitive closure", String(R.transitiveClosure()));
divisorLattice(30).isDistributive()
```

Page: https://ratmath.com/discrete/polya.html

Orders and structures

## Pólya counting

How many different necklaces of six beads in two colours are there, when turning or flipping a necklace gives the same one? Burnside's lemma counts orbits by averaging fixed points, and Pólya's cycle index makes that a polynomial you can substitute into.

### Burnside's lemma

A group G acting on a finite set has

#orbits=∣G∣1​g∈G∑​∣Fix(g)∣
orbits. For colourings of n positions with k colours, a permutation with c(g) cycles fixes kc(g) colourings, since each cycle must be one colour.

```js
import { symmetry, countColourings, cycleIndex, patternInventory } from "@ratmath/discrete";

countColourings(symmetry.cyclic(6), 2);      // 14n necklaces
countColourings(symmetry.dihedral(6), 2);    // 13n bracelets
countColourings(symmetry.cubeFaces(), 3);    // 57n ways to colour a cube's faces
```

### The cycle index

```js
cycleIndex(symmetry.dihedral(4)).toString();
// "(1/4) s4 + (1/4) s1^2 s2 + (3/8) s2^2 + (1/8) s1^4"
patternInventory(symmetry.dihedral(4), ["r", "b"]).toString();
// "r^4 + r^3b + 2r^2b^2 + rb^3 + b^4"
```

The cycle index records the cycle type of every group element: Z(G)=∣G∣1​∑g​∏i​sici​(g)​, where ci​(g) is the number of i-cycles. Substituting si​=k gives the count above. Substituting si​=ri+bi gives the pattern inventory, which counts orbits by how many of each colour they use: the square has two different colourings with two red and two blue corners, adjacent or opposite.

### Groups

`symmetry` provides the cyclic, dihedral and symmetric groups and the 24 rotations of a cube acting on its faces. Any group works when given as `{ degree, generators }` with 0-based permutations, or as a `PermGroup` from `@ratmath/algebraic`, such as the automorphism group of a graph from [Isomorphism and spectra](https://ratmath.com/discrete/isomorphism-spectra.html).

### Try it

```js
// Burnside's count against listing orbits directly.
const orbits = (G, k) => {
  const seen = new Set();
  let count = 0;
  for (const col of words(k, G.degree)) {
    const key = col.join();
    if (seen.has(key)) continue;
    count++;
    for (const g of G.elements) { const img = []; g.forEach((gi, i) => (img[gi] = col[i])); seen.add(img.join()); }
  }
  return count;
};
for (const [name, G, k] of [["necklaces C6, 2", symmetry.cyclic(6), 2], ["bracelets D6, 3", symmetry.dihedral(6), 3], ["cube faces, 3", symmetry.cubeFaces(), 3]]) {
  PRINT(name.padEnd(16), "Pólya", String(countColourings(G, k)).padStart(4), "  listed", String(orbits(G, k)).padStart(4));
}
// Colourings of the Petersen graph's vertices in 2 colours, up to its 120 symmetries
const A = automorphisms(petersen());
PRINT("Petersen, 2 colours:", String(countColourings(A.group, 2)));
cycleIndex(symmetry.cubeFaces()).toString()
```

Page: https://ratmath.com/discrete/codes.html

Codes and designs

## Error-correcting codes

Add redundancy to a message so that a few corrupted symbols can be found and fixed. A linear code is a subspace of Zpn​; its minimum distance says how many errors it can correct, and its parity-check matrix says where they are.

### The Hamming code

```js
import { hammingCode, isPerfect } from "@ratmath/discrete";

const h = hammingCode(3);         // [7, 4] over Z_2
h.minimumDistance().distance;     // 3: corrects one error
isPerfect(h);                     // true
const cw = h.encode([1, 0, 1, 1]);   // [1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0]
h.decode([1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 0]).steps;
// ["received 1001010", "syndrome H·rᵀ = 110",
//  "the lightest error with that syndrome is 0010000 (weight 1)", "corrected codeword 1011010, message 1011"]
```

A code with generator matrix G (k×n) encodes m as mG. Put G in systematic form [Ik​∣A]; then H=[−A⊤∣In−k​] satisfies GH⊤=0, and a word r is a codeword exactly when its syndrome Hr⊤ is zero. If r=c+e, the syndrome is He⊤, so decoding is finding the lightest error with that syndrome, the coset leader. In the Hamming code the columns of H are all non-zero vectors, so the syndrome of a single error is its position written in binary.

### Distance and bounds

A code with minimum distance d corrects t=⌊(d−1)/2⌋ errors, because balls of radius t round the codewords do not overlap. Counting the words in those balls gives the Hamming (sphere-packing) bound, and a code that meets it is perfect:

∣C∣⋅i=0∑t​(in​)(q−1)i≤qn.

```js
import { codeBounds, ballSize } from "@ratmath/discrete";
codeBounds(7, 3, 2);   // { hamming: 16n, singleton: 32n, gilbertVarshamov: 5n }
ballSize(7, 1);        // 8n, and 16 · 8 = 2^7: the Hamming code is perfect
h.weightDistribution();             // [1, 0, 0, 7, 7, 0, 0, 1]
h.dual().minimumDistance().distance;   // 4: the [7, 3] simplex code
```

### Reed–Solomon

```js
import { reedSolomon } from "@ratmath/discrete";
const rs = reedSolomon({ p: 11, n: 10, k: 4 });   // corrects 3 errors
const w = rs.encode([3, 1, 4, 1]);                // the values of 3 + x + 4x² + x³ at 1, …, 10
const y = w.slice(); y[0] += 1; y[5] += 3; y[9] += 7;   // three errors (mod 11)
rs.decode(y.map((v) => v % 11)).errors;           // [0, 5, 9]
```

A message is a polynomial f of degree below k, sent as its values at n distinct points. Two such polynomials agree in at most k−1 places, so the distance is n−k+1, meeting the Singleton bound. Berlekamp–Welch decoding looks for an error locator E of degree e (monic) and Q of degree below e+k with Q(αi​)=yi​E(αi​) for every i: a linear system over Zp​. Then f=Q/E, and E vanishes at the error positions. The steps show the system, E, Q and the division.

### Try it

```js
// Every single-bit error in every Hamming(3) codeword is corrected.
const h = hammingCode(3);
let fixed = 0, total = 0;
for (const m of words(2, 4)) {
  const cw = h.encode(m);
  for (let i = 0; i < 7; i++) {
    const r = cw.slice(); r[i] ^= 1; total++;
    if (h.decode(r).codeword.join() === cw.join()) fixed++;
  }
}
PRINT(`${fixed} of ${total} single errors corrected`);
// Ternary Hamming code and Reed–Solomon with random errors
const h3 = hammingCode(2, { p: 3 });
PRINT(String(h3), " d =", h3.minimumDistance().distance, " perfect:", isPerfect(h3));
const rs = reedSolomon({ p: 13, n: 12, k: 6 });
const r = rng("reed-solomon");
const msg = Array.from({ length: 6 }, () => r.int(13));
const y = rs.encode(msg);
for (const i of r.sample([...Array(12).keys()], 3)) y[i] = (y[i] + 1 + r.int(12)) % 13;
const d = rs.decode(y);
PRINT("sent", msg.join(" "), " decoded", d.message.join(" "), " errors at", d.errors.join(", "));
codeBounds(23, 7, 2)
```

Page: https://ratmath.com/discrete/designs.html

Codes and designs

## Latin squares and designs

A design arranges points into blocks so that every pair of points meets equally often. Latin squares, finite geometries and Steiner triple systems are all designs, and their existence is a question about arithmetic in finite fields.

### Latin squares

```js
import { cyclicLatinSquare, isLatinSquare, orthogonalLatinSquares, areOrthogonal } from "@ratmath/discrete";

isLatinSquare(cyclicLatinSquare(6));   // { latin: true, problem: null }
const L = orthogonalLatinSquares(5);    // 4 squares: L_a[i][j] = a·i + j mod 5
areOrthogonal(L[0], L[1]);              // { orthogonal: true, repeated: null }
```

Each symbol appears once in every row and column. Two squares are orthogonal when superimposing them gives every ordered pair of symbols exactly once. For a prime p, the squares La​(i,j)=ai+j with a=1,…,p−1 are mutually orthogonal, since ai+j=ai′+j′ and bi+j=bi′+j′ force i=i′ when a=b. At most n−1 squares of order n can be mutually orthogonal, so this is a complete set. Euler's 36 officers (n=6) have no orthogonal pair at all.

### Block designs

```js
import { blockDesign, projectivePlane, affinePlane, fromDifferenceSet, steinerTripleSystem } from "@ratmath/discrete";
const fano = blockDesign(projectivePlane(2));
[fano.v, fano.b, fano.k, fano.r, fano.lambda];   // [7, 7, 3, 3, 1]: the Fano plane
blockDesign(fromDifferenceSet([1, 3, 4, 5, 9], 11)).lambda;   // 2: the squares mod 11
blockDesign(steinerTripleSystem(15)).b;          // 35 triples
```

A (v,k,λ) design has v points and blocks of size k, with every pair of points in exactly λ blocks. Counting pairs gives the necessary conditions

bk=vr,r(k−1)=λ(v−1),
and Fisher's inequality b≥v. `blockDesign` computes v,b,k,r,λ from the blocks and checks these relations, returning `lambda: null` when pairs are not balanced.

### Finite geometry

The projective plane of order p has the one-dimensional subspaces of Zp3​ as points and the two-dimensional ones as lines: p2+p+1 of each, p+1 points on a line, and any two points on exactly one line. Removing one line and its points leaves the affine plane, p2 points in p2+p lines. A difference set D⊂Zv​, where every non-zero residue is a difference of elements of D exactly λ times, gives a design with blocks D+i. Steiner triple systems (k=3, λ=1) exist exactly when v≡1 or 3(mod6); Bose's construction covers v≡3.

### Try it

```js
// Parameters of some designs, and the counting identities they satisfy.
const designs = [["Fano plane", projectivePlane(2)], ["PG(2,3)", projectivePlane(3)], ["AG(2,3)", affinePlane(3)], ["AG(2,5)", affinePlane(5)], ["STS(9)", steinerTripleSystem(9)], ["STS(15)", steinerTripleSystem(15)], ["QR(11)", fromDifferenceSet([1, 3, 4, 5, 9], 11)], ["(13,4,1)", fromDifferenceSet([0, 1, 3, 9], 13)]];
for (const [name, B] of designs) {
  const d = blockDesign(B);
  PRINT(name.padEnd(10), `v=${d.v} b=${d.b} k=${d.k} r=${d.r} λ=${d.lambda}`, " bk=vr:", d.b * d.k === d.v * d.r, " r(k−1)=λ(v−1):", d.r * (d.k - 1) === d.lambda * (d.v - 1));
}
// The Fano plane's lines, and a complete set of orthogonal Latin squares of order 7
PRINT(projectivePlane(2).map((l) => l.join("")).join(" "));
const L = orthogonalLatinSquares(7);
PRINT(L.length, "squares, pairwise orthogonal:", L.every((A, i) => L.every((B, j) => i === j || areOrthogonal(A, B).orthogonal)));
blockDesign(affinePlane(7))
```
